title: Rotated Digits
approach_name: Validate digits and track a changed digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotated Digits requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `rotatedDigits` converts each candidate to a string, checks all characters against `good`, and requires at least one member of `changed`.
Technique and why it applies: The `good` set validates every digit, while `changed` ensures the rotation is not identical to the original number.
Invariant: `ans` counts candidates whose digits are all valid and whose value changes after rotation.
Edge cases: Digits 0, 1, and 8 are valid but unchanged; 3, 4, and 7 invalidate a candidate.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for n candidates and O(1) auxiliary set space.
complexity_reason: Both conditions matter: every digit must rotate legally, and at least one digit must map differently.

title: Rotated Digits
approach_name: Validate digits and track a changed digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotated Digits requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `rotatedDigits` extracts digits with `% 10`, rejects 3, 4, and 7, and sets `changed` for 2, 5, 6, or 9.
Technique and why it applies: Arithmetic digit extraction lets the method reject forbidden digits early and independently track whether any digit changes.
Invariant: `ans` counts candidates for which every examined digit is valid and at least one digit changes.
Edge cases: Digits 0, 1, and 8 are valid but unchanged; a forbidden digit stops the scan.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int rotatedDigits(int n){int ans=0;for(int x=1;x<=n;x++){int v=x;boolean valid=true,changed=false;while(v>0){int d=v%10;if(d==3||d==4||d==7){valid=false;break;}if(d==2||d==5||d==6||d==9)changed=true;v/=10;}if(valid&&changed)ans++;}return ans;} }
complexity_reason: The digit scan rejects invalid rotations and records whether a non-self-mapping digit occurs.

title: Rotate String
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate String requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `rotateString` checks equal lengths and searches for `goal` inside `s+s`.
Technique and why it applies: Every cyclic rotation is a contiguous window in `s+s`, so substring membership checks all possible rotations.
Invariant: For equal-length strings, every rotation appears as a length-n substring of the doubled string.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths return false immediately; identical strings return true; empty strings also match as valid zero-length rotations.
Complexity: O(n) typical time and O(n) space for the doubled string.
code:
class Solution:
 def rotateString(self,s,goal):return len(s)==len(goal) and goal in s+s
complexity_reason: Concatenating the string with itself exposes every rotation cut point as an ordinary substring.

title: Rotate String
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate String requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `rotateString` checks equal lengths before evaluating `(s+s).contains(goal)`.
Technique and why it applies: The doubled-string property converts a rotation test into one ordinary substring search after a length check.
Invariant: Equal-length candidates are rotations exactly when `goal` occurs in the doubled source.
Edge cases: Different lengths fail; empty strings match; a doubled string takes linear space.
Complexity: O(n) typical time and O(n) auxiliary string space.
code: class Solution { public boolean rotateString(String s,String goal){return s.length()==goal.length()&&(s+s).contains(goal);} }
complexity_reason: The length guard rules out impossible rotations before searching the doubled string.

title: Unique Morse Code Words
notes:
Task and constraints: Unique Morse Code Words requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `uniqueMorseRepresentations` maps each lowercase letter through the code array, joins each word's codes, and stores encodings in a set.
Technique and why it applies: The character-indexed code table builds deterministic encodings, and set membership removes duplicate encoded strings.
Invariant: The set contains exactly the distinct encodings encountered so far.
Edge cases: Different words may share an encoding; input letters are lowercase.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(total encoded characters) space.
complexity_reason: Set cardinality counts unique encodings even when different words map to the same Morse sequence.

title: Unique Morse Code Words
notes:
Task and constraints: Unique Morse Code Words requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `uniqueMorseRepresentations` appends each character code to a `StringBuilder`, inserts each encoding into a `HashSet`, and returns set size.
Technique and why it applies: A `StringBuilder` assembles each word's Morse symbols before hashing the completed representation for deduplication.
Invariant: The set contains one entry per distinct encoded word processed.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; collisions count once; letters are lowercase.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(total encoded characters) space.
code: class Solution { public int uniqueMorseRepresentations(String[] words){String[]c={".-","-...","-.-.","-..",".","..-.","--.","....","..",".---","-.-",".-..","--","-.","---",".--.","--.-",".-.","...","-","..-","...-",".--","-..-","-.--","--.."};java.util.Set<String>s=new java.util.HashSet<>();for(String w:words){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(char x:w.toCharArray())b.append(c[x-'a']);s.add(b.toString());}return s.size();} }
complexity_reason: The builder forms a complete code per word, and the set removes duplicate representations.

title: Number of Lines To Write String
notes:
Task and constraints: Number of Lines To Write String requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `numberOfLines` reads each character width and opens a new line when `cur+w > 100`; otherwise it adds to `cur`.
Technique and why it applies: The strict overflow condition preserves the 100-unit limit while greedily retaining each character in order.
Invariant: `cur` tracks the current line width and never exceeds 100.
Edge cases: Empty text returns `[1,0]`; width exactly 100 fits; letters are lowercase.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: A new line is opened only when adding the next letter would exceed 100 units.

title: Number of Lines To Write String
notes:
Task and constraints: Number of Lines To Write String requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `numberOfLines` looks up each letter width and resets `cur` to that width when `cur+w > 100`.
Technique and why it applies: Checking width before adding a character identifies the earliest legal line break without rearranging the string.
Invariant: `cur` is the used width of the current line and remains at most 100.
Edge cases: Empty input returns one line of width zero; width exactly 100 fits.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int[] numberOfLines(int[] widths,String s){int lines=1,cur=0;for(char c:s.toCharArray()){int w=widths[c-'a'];if(cur+w>100){lines++;cur=w;}else cur+=w;}return new int[]{lines,cur};} }
complexity_reason: The overflow check happens before addition, so no line's width exceeds the allowed maximum.

title: Subdomain Visit Count
approach_name: Accumulate counts for every suffix domain
notes:
Task and constraints: Subdomain Visit Count requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `subdomainVisits` splits domains into labels and adds each input count to every suffix formed by joining `parts[i:]`.
Technique and why it applies: Joining progressively shorter label suffixes updates both the full domain and each parent subdomain total.
Invariant: `counts[d]` is the accumulated visit total for domain `d` across processed records.
Edge cases: A multi-label domain contributes to every suffix; output order is not significant.
Complexity: Time proportional to generated suffixes and string construction; O(distinct subdomains) map space.
complexity_reason: Each input domain contributes its count to the full hostname and every suffix subdomain.

title: Subdomain Visit Count
approach_name: Accumulate counts for every suffix domain
notes:
Task and constraints: Subdomain Visit Count requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `subdomainVisits` parses each count and updates a map for every suffix of the domain labels.
Technique and why it applies: The nested suffix construction maps every specific hostname to all of its enclosing domain names.
Invariant: `m[d]` sums counts for all input domains whose suffix is `d`.
Edge cases: A single-label domain contributes only to itself; `HashMap` output order is unspecified.
Complexity: Time proportional to generated suffixes and their construction; O(distinct subdomains) map space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<String> subdomainVisits(String[] cpdomains){Map<String,Integer>m=new HashMap<>();for(String item:cpdomains){String[]p=item.split(" ");int n=Integer.parseInt(p[0]);String[]labels=p[1].split("\\.");for(int i=0;i<labels.length;i++){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int j=i;j<labels.length;j++){if(j>i)b.append('.');b.append(labels[j]);}m.put(b.toString(),m.getOrDefault(b.toString(),0)+n);}}List<String>out=new ArrayList<>();for(String d:m.keySet())out.add(m.get(d)+" "+d);return out;} }
complexity_reason: Building every suffix and adding the record's count computes both specific and parent-domain totals.

title: Most Common Word
approach_name: Normalize words and count allowed tokens
notes:
Task and constraints: Most Common Word requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `mostCommonWord` lowercases the paragraph, extracts `[a-z]+` tokens, filters banned words, and uses `Counter.most_common(1)`.
Technique and why it applies: The regular expression isolates alphabetic words, and the banned set filters normalized tokens before frequency ranking.
Invariant: The counter contains only normalized, non-banned tokens and their frequencies.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees an answer; punctuation-only text would leave no token.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for token counts.
complexity_reason: Lowercase tokenization normalizes punctuation and case before banned-word filtering and frequency ranking.

title: Most Common Word
approach_name: Normalize words and count allowed tokens
notes:
Task and constraints: Most Common Word requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `mostCommonWord` lowercases tokens, splits on nonletters, skips empty or banned words, and updates `best` only when a count exceeds `max`.
Technique and why it applies: Lowercase normalization and splitting on nonletters make punctuation irrelevant to the frequency map keys.
Invariant: `best` is a highest-frequency allowed word among processed tokens and `max` stores its count.
Edge cases: Empty split tokens are skipped; input guarantees a valid answer; ties keep the earlier winner.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public String mostCommonWord(String paragraph,String[] banned){Set<String>ban=new HashSet<>();for(String w:banned)ban.add(w.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT));Map<String,Integer>count=new HashMap<>();String best="";int max=0;for(String w:paragraph.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).split("[^a-z]+")){if(w.isEmpty()||ban.contains(w))continue;int n=count.getOrDefault(w,0)+1;count.put(w,n);if(n>max){max=n;best=w;}}return best;} }
complexity_reason: The strict count comparison keeps the earlier winner when counts tie.

title: Shortest Distance to a Character
notes:
Task and constraints: Shortest Distance to a Character requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `shortestToChar` fills distances from the last target in a forward pass, then minimizes them with distances from the next target in a backward pass.
Technique and why it applies: The forward scan computes left distances, and the reverse scan supplies right distances for a pointwise minimum.
Invariant: After the first pass each entry has its nearest left-side distance; after the second it has the nearest overall distance.
Edge cases: The target character is guaranteed to appear; sentinels cover positions outside the first and last target.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: The first pass handles left-side occurrences and the second improves results using right-side occurrences.

title: Shortest Distance to a Character
notes:
Task and constraints: Shortest Distance to a Character requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `shortestToChar` initializes a left sentinel, fills distances forward, and then minimizes them using a backward scan.
Technique and why it applies: Sentinel indices represent missing targets beyond the boundaries, allowing both passes to use uniform distance updates.
Invariant: The first pass measures nearest left targets; the second finalizes each nearest distance.
Edge cases: At least one target is guaranteed; sentinels avoid special cases at the ends.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[] shortestToChar(String s,char c){int n=s.length();int[]a=new int[n];int last=-n;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){if(s.charAt(i)==c)last=i;a[i]=i-last;}last=2*n;for(int i=n-1;i>=0;i--){if(s.charAt(i)==c)last=i;a[i]=Math.min(a[i],last-i);}return a;} }
complexity_reason: The right-to-left pass compares the stored left distance with the nearest right-side distance.

title: Goat Latin
notes:
Task and constraints: Goat Latin requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `toGoatLatin` enumerates words from one, moves a consonant-leading first letter to the end, and appends `ma` plus that many `a` characters.
Technique and why it applies: The initial-character vowel test selects the move, while the one-based enumeration controls the appended suffix length.
Invariant: Each output word follows the vowel/consonant rule and has a suffix matching its one-based position.
Edge cases: Vowel-leading words keep their order; words are assumed non-empty; output uses single spaces.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space, counting appended suffixes.
complexity_reason: Enumerating words from one makes the number of appended `a` characters match each word's position.

title: Goat Latin
notes:
Task and constraints: Goat Latin requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `toGoatLatin` splits words, checks `vowels.indexOf`, moves consonant initials, appends `ma` and an index-sized repeated `a` suffix, then joins words.
Technique and why it applies: The vowel lookup chooses whether to rotate the first character, and the loop position controls repeated suffix characters.
Invariant: Each processed word has the prescribed transformation and one-based suffix length.
Edge cases: Vowel-leading words stay unchanged before suffixing; valid words are non-empty.
Complexity: O(n) time in input plus output characters and O(n) space.
code: class Solution { public String toGoatLatin(String sentence){String[]w=sentence.split(" ");StringBuilder out=new StringBuilder();String vowels="aeiouAEIOU";for(int i=0;i<w.length;i++){String x=w[i];if(vowels.indexOf(x.charAt(0))<0)x=x.substring(1)+x.charAt(0);x+="ma"+"a".repeat(i+1);if(i>0)out.append(' ');out.append(x);}return out.toString();} }
complexity_reason: The zero-based loop index plus one supplies the required suffix length for each word.

title: Positions of Large Groups
notes:
Task and constraints: Positions of Large Groups requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `largeGroupPositions` advances `j` through a maximal run, records `[i,j-1]` for length at least three, and resumes at `j`.
Technique and why it applies: Scanning to the first differing character identifies one maximal group and makes each character part of a single run.
Invariant: `i` begins the next unprocessed run and `j` is its first index after the run.
Edge cases: Empty strings return an empty list; exactly three equal characters qualify; endpoints are inclusive.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case output space.
complexity_reason: Advancing `i` directly to the first index after a run avoids rescanning its characters.

title: Positions of Large Groups
notes:
Task and constraints: Positions of Large Groups requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `largeGroupPositions` advances `j` while characters match `s.charAt(i)`, records `[i,j-1]` when length is at least three, and sets `i=j`.
Technique and why it applies: The inner loop discovers maximal run boundaries, so the next outer iteration starts at an unprocessed character.
Invariant: The inner loop ends at the first different character or the string end, leaving `i` at the next run.
Edge cases: Empty strings return no ranges; length-two runs are skipped; end indices are inclusive.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public List<List<Integer>> largeGroupPositions(String s){List<List<Integer>>out=new ArrayList<>();int i=0;while(i<s.length()){int j=i;while(j<s.length()&&s.charAt(j)==s.charAt(i))j++;if(j-i>=3)out.add(Arrays.asList(i,j-1));i=j;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: The inner scan consumes a complete run before the outer loop begins another.

title: Flipping an Image
notes:
Task and constraints: Flipping an Image requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `flipAndInvertImage` reverses each row with `row[::-1]` and XORs each bit with one.
Technique and why it applies: A reversed row slice fixes horizontal order before XOR complements each binary value in the resulting row.
Invariant: Every output row is the reversed input row with all binary values complemented.
Edge cases: Empty matrices return empty output; input values are binary.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space.
complexity_reason: Reversing first and XORing each bit produces the required mirrored, inverted row.

title: Flipping an Image
notes:
Task and constraints: Flipping an Image requires the transformation or count described by its problem, preserving the input's specified ordering and constraints.
Idea: `flipAndInvertImage` assigns `image[i][n-1-j] ^ 1` into each output position.
Technique and why it applies: Reading column `n-1-j` mirrors the row, and XOR with one converts zero to one or one to zero.
Invariant: Output `(i,j)` is the inverse of the input at `(i,n-1-j)`.
Edge cases: Empty outer input returns empty output; input is rectangular and binary under constraints.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[][] flipAndInvertImage(int[][] image){int[][]out=new int[image.length][];for(int i=0;i<image.length;i++){int n=image[i].length;out[i]=new int[n];for(int j=0;j<n;j++)out[i][j]=image[i][n-1-j]^1;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: The mirrored source index handles reversal, and XOR one performs bit inversion.
